\section[o efeito]{o efeito — the effect}

\label{lesson:PT-C348-efeito}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to rebut, then the Portuguese for relevant.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o efeito}
\textbf{o efeito} — \textquotedblleft{}the effect\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O remédio fez efeito depressa.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The medicine took effect quickly.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Fazer efeito} — to take effect; \emph{com efeito} — indeed.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{efeito} is inherited from Latin \emph{effectus} \textquotedblleft{}an effect, a result\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), from \emph{efficere} \textquotedblleft{}to bring about\textquotedblright{}, built from \emph{ex} and \emph{facere} \textquotedblleft{}to do, to make\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short); \emph{-ct-} became \emph{-it-} as in \emph{feito}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{o efeito}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{o efeito}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{o efeito}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for to rebut, then the Portuguese for relevant, then say \emph{o efeito} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does o efeito mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The effect\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[provocar]{provocar — to bring about, to cause; to provoke}

\label{lesson:PT-C348-provocar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for relevant, then the Portuguese for the effect.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: provocar}
\textbf{provocar} — \textquotedblleft{}to bring about, to cause; to provoke\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
A chuva forte provocou muitos acidentes.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The heavy rain caused many accidents.}
\end{quote}

Also to provoke or tease a person.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{provocar} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{prōvocāre} \textquotedblleft{}to call forth, to call out, to challenge\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB, Lewis \& Short), built from \emph{prō} and \emph{vocāre} \textquotedblleft{}to call\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{provocar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{provocar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{provocar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for relevant, then the Portuguese for the effect, then say \emph{provocar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[causar]{causar — to cause}

\label{lesson:PT-C348-causar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the effect, then the Portuguese for to bring about.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: causar}
\textbf{causar} — \textquotedblleft{}to cause\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O acidente causou muito trânsito.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The accident caused a lot of traffic.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Causar problemas} — to cause problems.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{causar} is built on \emph{causa} \textquotedblleft{}cause\textquotedblright{} with the verb ending \emph{-ar} (EtymDB); \emph{causa} comes from Latin \emph{causa} \textquotedblleft{}reason, cause, lawsuit\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[o fator]{o fator — the factor}

\label{lesson:PT-C348-fator}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to bring about, then the Portuguese for to cause.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o fator}
\textbf{o fator} — \textquotedblleft{}the factor\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O preço é um fator importante na escolha.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The price is an important factor in the choice.}
\end{quote}

European \emph{fator} (AO90); older spelling \emph{factor}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{fator} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{factor} \textquotedblleft{}a maker, a doer, a performer\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB, Lewis \& Short), from \emph{facere} \textquotedblleft{}to make\textquotedblright{}; Portuguese also has the inherited form \emph{feitor} \textquotedblleft{}steward\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[a consequência]{a consequência — the consequence}

\label{lesson:PT-C348-consequencia}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to cause, then the Portuguese for the factor.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a consequência}
\textbf{a consequência} — \textquotedblleft{}the consequence\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Ele não pensou nas consequências.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{He did not think about the consequences.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Em consequência de} — as a result of.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{consequência} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{cōnsequentia} \textquotedblleft{}a consequence, a natural succession\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB, Lewis \& Short), from \emph{cōnsequī} \textquotedblleft{}to follow after\textquotedblright{}, built on \emph{sequī} \textquotedblleft{}to follow\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
